g: Romantic fantasy (romantasy); enemies-to-lovers with Regency-style manners and magic
sum: Two heirs of feuding magical families have been raised to despise each other, and their rivalry is as much public spectacle as private grudge. When circumstances force them into close quarters and a shared goal, barbed wit becomes the only safe way to speak, and every exchange carries more feeling than either is prepared to admit, to the other or to themselves.
bg: Brigitte Knightley’s debut novel opens the two-book Dearly Beloathed series. It belongs to the recent wave of witty, banter-led romantic fantasies that borrow the ballrooms, chaperones and social stakes of Regency romance and set them inside an invented world with its own magic, families and politics. The sequel, The Exquisite Torment of Loving Your Enemy, completes the story.
br: Read it as a comedy of manners first. The pleasure lies in the sparring and in the gap between what the two leads say and what they do. The world is sketched lightly on purpose: the relationship is the engine, and the magic and politics exist mainly to put pressure on it.
la: Knightley stays close to both leads, so the reader watches each misread the other and enjoys knowing more than either of them. She relies on rapid dialogue, social set pieces where reputation is at stake, and the slow-burn convention of delayed admission, where the emotional payoff depends on how long it is withheld.
cx: Enemies-to-lovers is one of the most popular romance tropes in recent publishing, boosted by online reading communities. This duology plays with the trope’s conventions knowingly rather than reinventing them, which is part of its appeal as comfort reading.
th: Pride and inheritance
Family loyalty can feel like identity and like a cage at the same time.
Performance and sincerity
A public rivalry gives both leads cover to pay each other close attention.
Choosing your own story
Each heir has to decide which parts of the family script to keep.
fit: A deliberate palate cleanser between heavier philosophy and history: quick, funny and warm, and positioned in your reading order for exactly that.
mis: Readers who want dense worldbuilding or serious political stakes may find the setting thin, and open-door romance scenes are part of the genre.
rq: What does each lead gain from keeping the rivalry alive?
Where does the banter hide something unsaid?
How much of the feud belongs to the parents rather than the children?
dq: Which romance conventions does the book play straight, and which does it tease?
Would the story work without magic at all?

sum: The second Dearly Beloathed novel returns to the pair whose rivalry has turned into something much harder to name. Having admitted more than they meant to, they now face the consequences from their families, from society, and from the magical stakes left unresolved at the end of the first book. The question is no longer whether they feel it but what they will risk for it.
bg: Brigitte Knightley’s follow-up completes the duology begun in The Irresistible Urge to Fall for Your Enemy. Because it picks up directly from the first book’s turning points, this profile stays deliberately vague about plot. Two-book arcs like this are common in romantic fantasy, giving a contained story with a definite ending.
br: Read it after the first book; it assumes you know the characters and the state of the feud. Expect the focus to shift from will-they to how-will-they: commitment under pressure rather than the thrill of attraction, with the humour still running underneath.
la: Sequels in this genre often trade the first book’s sparring for vulnerability. Watch how Knightley keeps the comic voice while letting the leads be wrong in new ways, and how she turns external obstacles back into questions about trust and loyalty.
cx: Placed in your plan as a matching bookend to the first volume, it gives a clean sense of a finished series, a useful contrast to the long multi-book fantasy arcs elsewhere in your year.
th: Trust after confession
Saying the feeling aloud is the beginning of the problem, not the end of it.
Divided loyalty
Love asks for choices that families may never forgive.
Growing up
The leads have to become adults in their own right rather than heirs.
fit: Completes a light, comic duology and rounds off a story you will already be invested in from earlier in the year.
mis: If the first book’s banter and tropes did not land for you, the sequel offers more of the same tone and structure.
rq: What has changed in how the two speak to each other?
Which obstacles are external and which are self-made?
What would a satisfying ending owe each character?
dq: Does the conclusion resolve the feud or simply outgrow it?
How does the sequel change your view of the first book?

g: Literary fantasy; mystery told through a journal
sum: Piranesi lives in an immense House of endless halls, marble statues and tides that flood the lower floors. He records its patterns with devotion and believes himself one of only two living people in the world. His only regular company is a man he calls the Other. Small inconsistencies in his own journals begin to suggest that the world he loves has a history he cannot remember.
bg: Susanna Clarke’s second novel was published in 2020, sixteen years after Jonathan Strange & Mr Norrell, and won the 2021 Women’s Prize for Fiction. Clarke has spoken about writing it during years of chronic illness that kept her largely at home, and the book’s sense of a vast, solitary but beloved world reflects that.
br: Go in knowing as little as possible. Let the House’s rules reveal themselves, and pay attention to dates, names and journal index entries: the structure rewards careful reading, and the mystery is solved by noticing.
la: Clarke uses a narrator whose innocence and precision are both genuine, so the reader understands more than he does without ever feeling superior to him. The prose has the clarity of a naturalist’s field notebook, and wonder is built from exact description rather than ornament.
cx: The novel draws on classical statuary, labyrinth myth, C. S. Lewis’s The Magician’s Nephew and the twentieth-century figure of the charismatic occult scholar. It was widely read during the 2020 lockdowns, when its themes of confinement and attention resonated strongly.
th: Wonder and attention
Loving a place means noticing it precisely and without wanting to use it.
Memory and identity
A self can be lost and rebuilt from what remains.
Knowledge and exploitation
Some seekers want to master mystery rather than honour it.
fit: A natural bridge between your fantasy and philosophy shelves: brief, beautiful and contemplative, and a good reset after long series.
mis: Readers who need brisk plot from the first page may find the opening slow and puzzling until the mystery takes shape.
rq: What does Piranesi value that the Other ignores?
Which journal details seem out of place, and why?
Is the House a prison, a temple or both?
dq: What does the novel suggest about solitude and happiness?
How does the ending reframe what it means to be rescued?
rel: Clarke’s earlier, much longer novel of English magic.

sum: Genly Ai, an envoy from an interstellar alliance, arrives alone on the frozen planet Gethen to invite its nations to join. Gethenians have no fixed sex, and Genly’s assumptions about gender, politics and trust keep failing him. Court intrigue in one country gives way to exile, imprisonment and a dangerous journey across a glacier with the one person he least understands.
bg: Ursula K. Le Guin’s novel won both the Hugo and Nebula awards and is regarded as a landmark of science fiction. It belongs to her loosely connected Hainish Cycle, but stands entirely on its own; no other book is needed to follow it.
br: The opening chapters are deliberately disorienting, mixing official reports, myths, court politics and unfamiliar terms. Patience pays off: the second half becomes an intimate survival story and one of the great friendships in the genre.
la: Le Guin frames the book as a field report, interleaving Genly’s narrative with folk tales, religious texts and another character’s journal, so the reader assembles the culture as an anthropologist would. The prose is restrained and precise, and its emotional force builds slowly.
cx: Written at the height of second-wave feminism, the novel was both praised and debated for how it handles gender. Le Guin later revisited her own choices, including the use of he for Gethenians, in an essay called Is Gender Necessary? and its revised version.
th: Gender and perception
Much of what Genly sees on Gethen is what he expects to see.
Loyalty and betrayal
Patriotism and personal faith pull in opposite directions.
Duality and wholeness
Light and dark are parts of one thing rather than opposites.
fit: Pairs well with the Earthsea books already on your plan and with your philosophy reading on ethics and identity.
mis: The political chapters can feel dense and slow, and the cool, reportorial tone is not for every reader.
rq: What does Genly misunderstand first, and why?
How does shifgrethor shape conversation and trust?
What changes between the two travellers on the ice?
dq: Has the book’s treatment of gender aged well?
What is the novel’s idea of friendship?
rel: Le Guin’s fantasy counterpart in your plan.

sum: Socrates and his companions try to define justice and, to see it written large, imagine an ideal city from the ground up. Along the way the dialogue takes up education, the structure of the soul, the dangers of poetry, the rule of philosopher-kings, the decline of political systems, and the allegory of the cave, perhaps the most famous image in philosophy.
bg: Plato’s longest and most influential dialogue was written in Athens in the fourth century BCE, with his teacher Socrates as the main speaker. Its ten books range across ethics, politics, psychology, metaphysics and aesthetics, and much of later Western philosophy can be read as a response to it.
br: Read a book at a time, and keep the opening challenge in view: why be just if injustice pays? A good modern translation with notes, such as Grube revised by Reeve or Bloom, helps a great deal with names and references.
la: Plato writes drama as much as argument. Characters lose their tempers, concede too easily or push back hard, and the reader is invited to judge the arguments rather than simply accept them. Myths and images often carry the ideas that argument cannot.
cx: The Republic was composed after Athens lost the Peloponnesian War and executed Socrates. Its deep suspicion of democracy, and its proposals for censorship and rigid classes, are points modern readers argue with as much as admire.
th: Justice and the soul
A just city mirrors a well-ordered person in whom reason governs.
Education and power
Who should rule depends on who has been taught to see truly.
Appearance and reality
The cave asks what we mistake for the real world.
fit: Foundational for nearly every philosophy title later in your plan, especially Aristotle’s ethics and the political theory of Rousseau and Rawls.
mis: Long, and some sections, especially on censorship and social engineering, can feel authoritarian or repetitive.
cw: Discussion of eugenic breeding policies, censorship and infanticide in the ideal city.
rq: Is Thrasymachus actually answered, or merely silenced?
What does the cave allegory claim about education?
Where does the ideal city sacrifice freedom for order?
dq: Would you want to live in Plato’s city?
Which argument in the Republic has aged best?
